title: HAS “LOVE EVERYONE” BEEN TWISTED INTO “AFFIRM EVERYTHING”? JESUS NEVER ASKED YOU TO CHOOSE BETWEEN LOVE AND TRUTH.
paragraphs: HAS “LOVE EVERYONE” BEEN TWISTED INTO “AFFIRM EVERYTHING”? JESUS NEVER ASKED YOU TO CHOOSE BETWEEN LOVE AND TRUTH.

The most dangerous counterfeit of Christian love may not look like hatred. It may look like compassion that has quietly stopped calling anyone to repentance. But before you point at the world, there is something Jesus wants to confront in your own heart.
There is a kind of love being preached today that sounds so beautiful, so welcoming, so compassionate, that questioning it almost makes you feel cruel.
“Just love people.”
“Don't judge anyone.”
“God accepts everyone.”
“Who are you to tell someone how to live?”
And somewhere along the way, a dangerous assumption slipped into the conversation.
If you really love someone, you must affirm everything about them.
Their choices. Their desires. Their beliefs. Their relationships. Their version of truth. Even the things Scripture calls sin.
And if you dare disagree?
You're hateful.
You're judgmental.
You're religious.
You're unloving.
When did loving someone begin to mean agreeing with everything that could destroy them?
And perhaps an even more uncomfortable question...
Have we become so afraid of offending people that we are willing to remain silent about the very truth that could lead them to Christ?
Before you answer, understand something.
This is not an invitation to become harsh, arrogant, self-righteous, or cruel.
Some Christians have used biblical truth like a weapon and then wondered why wounded people ran away from the Church.
Some have publicly condemned sins they privately practiced.
Some have demanded repentance without ever demonstrating mercy.
Some have spoken about holiness with such contempt that the broken could barely recognize the Savior they claimed to represent.
That is not the heart of Jesus either.
Because the real question is not whether we should love people.
Jesus already settled that.
The question is whether we have allowed the world's changing definition of love to replace the love revealed in Jesus Christ.
And the answer matters more than our reputation, our popularity, our comfort, or the approval of the crowd.
It matters because eternity is real.
Sin is real.
Grace is real.
And the Cross was not necessary because humanity simply needed more affirmation.
The Cross was necessary because humanity needed redemption.
Imagine a woman standing in the middle of a crowd.
Her private failure has become public entertainment.
There are angry faces everywhere.
Religious men are demanding judgment.
Nobody is asking about her wounds.
Nobody is wondering how she got there.
Nobody seems interested in restoration.
To them, she is no longer a person.
She is a scandal.
And in the middle of that scandal stands Jesus.
John 8:1–11 records the account of a woman brought before Jesus after being accused of adultery. The religious leaders want to use her case to trap Him.
They know the Law.
They know the accusation.
They have already prepared their condemnation.
But Jesus does something nobody expects.
He stoops down.
He writes on the ground.
And when they continue pressing Him, He answers:
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” (John 8:7, KJV)
One by one, the accusers leave.
The crowd that came prepared to condemn suddenly has to confront its own guilt.
Then Jesus speaks to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Read that again.
Slowly.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy.
And moral truth.
Compassion.
And a call to change.
Jesus did not join the crowd in humiliating her.
But neither did He tell her that adultery was suddenly righteous because she had been wounded, exposed, or misunderstood.
He refused to reduce her to her sin.
And He refused to redefine her sin as holiness.
That is the difference between biblical love and counterfeit affirmation.
One sees a person worth rescuing.
The other can become so concerned with making a person feel accepted that it forgets the need for rescue altogether.

There is an important detail we should not ignore. The account of the woman caught in adultery, traditionally found in John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel. Many modern Bible translations identify this textual question. Christians have treasured the passage for centuries, but responsible interpretation acknowledges the manuscript evidence rather than hiding it.
And the beautiful truth is that the mercy and holiness illustrated in this account are firmly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
Jesus welcomed sinners.
Jesus called sinners to repentance.
Jesus offered forgiveness.
Jesus transformed lives.
He never treated people as disposable.
And He never treated sin as harmless.
That is not a contradiction.
That is the Gospel.
Consider the Greek language of the New Testament.
In John 1:14, Jesus is described as πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (plērēs charitos kai alētheias).
The phrase means “full of grace and truth.”
Not half grace and half truth.
Not grace when it is convenient and truth when someone irritates us.
Not grace for our own failures and harsh judgment for everybody else's.
Full of both.
Grace does not require dishonesty.
Truth does not require cruelty.
And Jesus embodies both perfectly.
Now consider Paul's words in Ephesians 4:15.
The Greek expression ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν ἀγάπῃ (alētheuontes de en agapē) is commonly translated “speaking the truth in love.”
The verb carries the idea of being truthful, not merely winning arguments with correct statements.
And the word ἀγάπῃ (agapē) refers to love in the context of the passage.
The instruction is not permission to say anything we want as long as we attach the phrase “I'm speaking the truth.”
It calls believers to grow into Christ through truthfulness expressed in love.
Because truth without love can become a weapon in sinful hands.
And love without truth can become an excuse to leave someone in bondage.
But Christlike love refuses both distortions.
Perhaps you have experienced the first one.
Maybe you grew up in a church where people noticed your clothing before they noticed your tears.
Where your mistakes became gossip.
Where your questions were treated like rebellion.
Where leaders spoke loudly about holiness but quietly ignored their own hypocrisy.
Maybe you heard more about what was wrong with you than about the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
And somewhere in your pain, you began to believe that anyone who spoke about repentance was simply another person preparing to reject you.
If that is your story, please hear this.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy that wounded you.
He is not the cruelty that embarrassed you.
He is not the spiritual arrogance that made you feel worthless.
The same Lord who confronts sin also condemns religious hypocrisy.
In Matthew 23, Jesus speaks some of His strongest rebukes to religious leaders who burden others while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
The Bible does not give Christians permission to disguise pride as righteousness.
And if we use truth to humiliate people, we are not becoming more like Jesus.
We are revealing how desperately we still need Him.
But there is another side to this conversation.
And it may be even harder to hear.
Maybe you have spent years using the word love to avoid an uncomfortable obedience.
You know what Scripture says.
You know what the Lord has been confronting in your heart.
But you have learned to soften every warning until nothing remains that challenges you.
You call conviction “negativity.”
You call correction “judgment.”
You call repentance “shame.”
You call biblical boundaries “hate.”
And because God is loving, you assume He must approve of whatever makes you happy.
But what if your happiness and your holiness are not always pointing in the same direction?
What if the very thing you are asking God to bless is something He is calling you to surrender?
What if His refusal to affirm a destructive choice is not evidence that He has stopped loving you...
But evidence that His love is too faithful to abandon you to it?
Hebrews 12:6 says:
“For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth...” (KJV)
The Greek verb παιδεύει (paideuei) speaks of training, instruction, and discipline.
It is not a picture of God taking pleasure in humiliating His children.
The passage describes a Father's purposeful discipline.
The love of God is not passive indifference.
He cares too much to leave His children unchanged.
Think about a father standing beside a road.
His little boy is running toward traffic.
The child is laughing.
He feels free.
He does not understand the danger.
Would a loving father simply smile and say, “I affirm your journey”?
Would he remain silent because stopping the child might upset him?
No.
He would call out.
He might even run after him.
Not because he hates his son.
Because he loves him.
Of course, human parents can misunderstand danger, and Christians can misunderstand Scripture. That is why our convictions must be examined carefully and humbly in the light of God's Word.
But the principle remains.
Love is not measured only by how comfortable someone feels in our presence. Love also seeks their genuine good.
And Scripture gives us an unmistakable test.
First Corinthians 13:6 says that love:
“Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth.” (KJV)
The Greek text reads:
οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ, συγχαίρει δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ
ou chairei epi tē adikia, synchairei de tē alētheia.
In context, it means love does not rejoice over wrongdoing or unrighteousness but rejoices together with the truth.
That is devastating to the idea that Christian love requires unconditional approval of every behavior.
Paul does not say love celebrates whatever a person sincerely desires.
He says love does not rejoice in unrighteousness.
Yet the very same chapter teaches that love is patient and kind, is not arrogant, does not insist on its own way, and does not keep a resentful record of wrongs.
We cannot quote verse 6 while ignoring verses 4 and 5.
If our supposed defense of righteousness makes us arrogant, rude, or delighted by someone else's downfall, we have violated the very passage we claim to defend.
And if our supposed compassion celebrates what God calls sin, we have also departed from its teaching.
This is where the Church must recover something we have too often lost.
The courage to tell the truth with tears in our eyes instead of stones in our hands.
Jesus did not build His ministry on the approval of crowds.
He touched lepers.
He ate with tax collectors.
He welcomed those society considered morally compromised.
He spoke with the Samaritan woman at the well, despite the social and religious barriers surrounding that encounter.
In John 4, He knew the complicated history of her relationships.
He did not pretend that her circumstances were irrelevant.
But neither did He treat her as unworthy of conversation.
He offered her living water.
And that encounter changed the direction of her story.
She arrived at the well carrying a water jar.
She left telling her community about Jesus.
The Savior who knew her history offered her something her history could never provide.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
Jesus already knows.
The relationship you keep justifying.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The secret addiction.
The dishonest business practice.
The resentment toward your family.
The sexual compromise.
The pride hiding behind your ministry.
The unforgiveness you have rehearsed for years.
The private life that contradicts your public worship.
The things you have learned to explain away because confronting them would require change.
He knows.
And still, He calls you to Himself.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because you matter enough that He came to save you from it.
There is a difference between being loved while you are a sinner and being told that sin needs no forgiveness.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Notice when Christ died for us.
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we mastered every spiritual discipline.
Not after we had something impressive to offer God.
While we were sinners.
But notice what His love accomplished.
He did not die to declare sin meaningless.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
The Greek word ἁμαρτωλῶν (hamartōlōn) in Romans 5:8 means “sinners.”
Paul is not describing humanity as a group of misunderstood people who simply need validation.
He is describing people who need the saving mercy of God.
And that includes every one of us.
The self-righteous preacher.
The exhausted single mother.
The successful businessman.
The person struggling with sexual temptation.
The church volunteer hiding an addiction.
The young believer afraid to confess doubt.
The person who has never stepped inside a church.
The Christian who knows every Bible verse but has forgotten how to love.
No one stands above the need for grace.
Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
And Romans 6:23 announces both the wages of sin and the gift of eternal life through Jesus Christ.
That is why we must be careful with the phrase “God accepts everyone.”
If by that we mean that people from every background are invited to come to Jesus, absolutely.
If we mean no sinner is beyond the reach of His mercy, absolutely.
If we mean we must treat every human being with dignity, compassion, and genuine love, absolutely.
But if we mean that God declares every belief, desire, and behavior righteous simply because a person sincerely embraces it, that is not the teaching of Scripture.
Jesus says in Mark 1:15:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The Greek verb μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) means “repent,” calling for a change of mind and direction in response to God's kingdom.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered your sin.
It is turning toward God in faith, acknowledging what is wrong, and abandoning the attempt to justify rebellion against Him.
And repentance is not the price we pay to purchase salvation.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith, as Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches.
But saving grace does not leave us indifferent to holiness.
It begins a new life in which we learn to walk in the good works God has prepared for us.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is the mercy of God meeting us in our helplessness and transforming us through Christ.
And that brings us to a painful reality in modern Christian culture.
Sometimes we have confused being welcoming with being unwilling to disagree.
We are afraid that if we speak about sin, people will leave.
We are afraid our friends will unfollow us.
We are afraid our children will think we hate them.
We are afraid our family members will stop inviting us to gatherings.
We are afraid that faithfulness to Scripture will cost us relationships we treasure.
And those fears are not imaginary.
Speaking truth can carry real consequences.
But we must also recognize that disagreement does not automatically make us faithful.
Sometimes our timing is wrong.
Sometimes our interpretation needs correction.
Sometimes we speak before listening.
Sometimes the wisest expression of love is to remain present, ask questions, and earn the trust necessary for an honest conversation.
We are not called to police every stranger's behavior.
First Corinthians 5:12–13 distinguishes the Church's responsibility to address sin within its own community from God's judgment of those outside it.
That distinction matters.
The Church must not demand that unbelievers perform Christian holiness before they have come to know Christ.
Nor should Christians assume that every moral disagreement is an opportunity for public confrontation.
Jesus calls His followers to make disciples, not to win every argument.
And discipleship requires patience.
Relationship.
Teaching.
Prayer.
Humility.
Consistency.
And the willingness to walk beside someone through a process of transformation that may take longer than we expected.
You can love someone who disagrees with your convictions.
You can honor their dignity without approving every decision.
You can listen without surrendering your beliefs.
You can maintain a relationship without pretending you share the same understanding of morality.
You can defend biblical teaching without mocking, demeaning, or mistreating people.
And you can admit when you have spoken wrongly without abandoning the truth you believe Scripture teaches.
This is not weakness.
This is spiritual maturity.
But there is another danger.
One that hides inside the heart of the person most eager to defend the truth.
It is possible to be doctrinally correct and spiritually cold.
It is possible to win an argument and lose an opportunity to demonstrate Christlike love.
It is possible to identify another person's sin while refusing to confront your own.
Remember the words of Jesus in Matthew 7:3–5.
Before trying to remove the speck from another person's eye, we must deal with the beam in our own.
Jesus is not teaching that moral discernment is forbidden.
He is confronting hypocrisy.
He teaches that we must address our own sin before attempting to help someone else.
That should humble every Christian who has ever felt superior because another person's failures were more visible.
The Cross leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
At Calvary, we discover two truths that human pride desperately wants to separate.
Our sin was serious enough that the Son of God gave His life for our redemption.
And God's love was great enough that He willingly gave His Son for sinners.
The Cross exposes sin.
And the Cross reveals love.
It does not minimize our guilt.
It announces the mercy that can overcome it.
When Jesus cried, “It is finished” in John 19:30, the Greek word recorded is τετέλεσται (tetelestai), from a verb meaning “to complete” or “bring to fulfillment.”
In John's account, Jesus has completed the work entrusted to Him as He gives up His life.
We should not reduce that sacred declaration to a motivational slogan.
It points to the completion of His saving mission through His sacrificial death.
And the story does not end in the tomb.
Jesus rose again.
The resurrection is God's triumphant declaration that death does not have the final word.
That is the center of Christian hope.
Not that we are perfect.
Not that our past was harmless.
Not that our sins were imaginary.
But that Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again, as Paul proclaims in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And because He lives, real transformation is possible.
The liar can learn to walk in truth.
The bitter heart can learn forgiveness.
The proud can become humble.
The addicted can seek help, receive support, and begin walking toward freedom.
The sexually broken can find grace, accountability, and a new way forward.
The religious hypocrite can repent.
The person who feels too far gone can discover that the mercy of Christ reaches farther than their shame.
Not every struggle disappears overnight.
Not every wound heals immediately.
And sincere believers may continue wrestling with temptation, trauma, grief, and deeply rooted habits.
But the Gospel gives us more than a new label.
It gives us a new Lord.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
That does not mean every consequence of the past vanishes.
It means our identity and future are no longer defined solely by the old life.
Christ has begun something new.
And perhaps the most scandalous part of grace is that Jesus is willing to begin that work in people we have already written off.
The person whose scandal became public.
The person whose marriage collapsed.
The person whose ministry failed.
The person who denied Christ under pressure.
The person who has wasted years.
The person who keeps returning to the same prayer with tears in their eyes.
The person who feels ashamed even to open a Bible.
If that person is you, hear the invitation of Jesus.
Come.
Not because your sin is acceptable.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because the Savior is merciful.
Come with the truth.
Come with the wounds.
Come with the confession you have been avoiding.
Come ready to surrender what God is calling you to surrender.
Come because the One who exposes our darkness is also the Light who can lead us out of it.
And if you have spent years standing in the crowd holding stones, come too.
Put down the contempt.
Put down the superiority.
Put down the secret satisfaction you feel when someone else's failure becomes public.
Repent of the cruelty you have excused in the name of defending God.
Because Jesus did not appoint us to become a community of merciless accusers.
He calls us to become people who have been forgiven and who therefore know how to extend mercy.
Galatians 6:1 tells spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in wrongdoing with gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
The Greek word καταρτίζετε (katartizete), translated “restore,” carries the idea of setting right or bringing back into proper condition.
The goal is restoration.
Not humiliation.
Not entertainment.
Not public destruction.
Restoration.
Imagine what our churches would look like if we took that seriously.
What if the person confessing an addiction found truthful accountability instead of gossip?
What if a young person asking difficult questions encountered patient biblical teaching instead of panic?
What if struggling marriages received compassionate support rather than whispered judgment?
What if people wrestling with sexual ethics heard both the Church's convictions and the unmistakable assurance that their dignity is not up for debate?
What if believers stopped using “love” as an excuse to ignore sin and stopped using “truth” as an excuse to mistreat sinners?
What if repentance was no longer treated as a word of rejection, but recognized as part of God's gracious invitation to return to Him?
What if the Church became a place where people could be honest about their struggles without being told those struggles define them forever?
That would not be a compromise of the Gospel.
That would be a community learning to live under its power.
And this is where the question becomes personal.
Not political.
Not cultural.
Not something you can safely aim at people on the other side of a screen.
Personal.
Are you loving people enough to tell the truth?
And equally important...
Are you loving people enough that they can recognize the heart of Jesus in the way you tell it?
Because if your truth is always loud but your compassion is never visible, something is wrong.
And if your compassion is always visible but you have decided that repentance is no longer necessary, something is also wrong.
Jesus is not asking you to choose between love and truth.
He is calling you to follow Him.
And following Him may cost you the approval of people who want affirmation without accountability.
It may also cost you the approval of religious people who want condemnation without compassion.
But the goal was never to please either crowd.
The goal is faithfulness to Christ.
There is someone reading this who has been struggling quietly.
You have been calling something harmless because admitting the truth would force you to change.
You have been praying for peace while resisting the obedience God has been placing before you.
You have been asking Jesus to comfort you without allowing His Word to correct you.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, you can feel the difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation tells you that you are hopeless.
The Gospel tells you that Christ is your hope.
Conviction exposes what needs to change.
Grace invites you to turn to the Savior who can change you.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
This promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a declaration that sin is insignificant.
It is the astonishing assurance that those united to Jesus are no longer under the condemning verdict of sin.
And Romans 8 goes on to describe life in the Spirit, where God's people are called away from the dominion of the flesh.
Freedom from condemnation is not freedom to celebrate bondage.
It is freedom to walk in newness of life.
So maybe your prayer tonight does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be sincere.

“Lord Jesus, I have confused Your patience with Your approval. I have excused things You have been calling me to surrender. And sometimes I have judged others without examining my own heart. Forgive me. Teach me to love what You love, reject what You call evil, and treat people with the mercy You have shown me. Give me courage to stand for truth without becoming cruel. Give me humility to receive correction without becoming defensive. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I trust in You. Change my heart. Lead me in Your ways. Amen.”
If you prayed those words sincerely, do not stop at an emotional moment.
Open your Bible.
Return to prayer.
Seek a faithful local church where Scripture is taught responsibly and people are cared for with humility.
Confess what needs to be confessed to God, and where appropriate seek the support and accountability of trustworthy believers.
If you have harmed someone, take responsible steps toward making things right.
If you are wrestling with a deeply rooted struggle, do not be ashamed to seek wise pastoral guidance and appropriate professional help.
Spiritual growth is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like choosing honesty when lying would be easier.
Sometimes it looks like turning off something you know is feeding temptation.
Sometimes it looks like apologizing without making excuses.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to join a conversation that humiliates someone who has fallen.
Sometimes it looks like staying faithful when nobody applauds.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible again after months of silence.
And sometimes it looks like whispering through tears...
“Jesus, I still need You.”
That is not the voice of someone beyond hope.
That is the cry of a soul learning where true hope is found.
And if this article has brought something to the surface that you have been hiding, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not need to expose private details or publicly confess something that should be handled with wisdom and confidentiality.
Your story may remind someone that repentance is not the end of hope.
It can be the beginning of restoration.
I also want to ask you to think of one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to win an argument against.
Someone you genuinely love.
Maybe a family member who has drifted away from faith.
Maybe a friend who believes Christianity is nothing but condemnation.
Maybe a believer who has confused compassion with compromise.
Maybe someone who has been so deeply wounded by religious hypocrisy that they can no longer imagine a Christianity full of both truth and mercy.
Or send the article privately with a simple message:
“I thought of you while reading this. I hope it encourages you.”
Not to create another argument.
Not to prove that you are more righteous than anyone else.
But because the Gospel deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our familiar circles.
A thoughtful share may reach someone who would never search for a Christian article on their own.
A family member.
An old friend.
A struggling believer.
A person who has been quietly wondering whether Jesus could ever welcome someone with their history.

There may come a day when you need to remember that truth is not the enemy of love, that repentance is not the enemy of grace, and that Jesus has never required you to abandon compassion in order to remain faithful.
We want this community to be more than a place where people read something emotional and move on.
We want it to become a place where biblical truth leads to prayer, repentance, healing, accountability, and a deeper walk with Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help people study the Bible, strengthen their faith, deepen their prayer lives, and develop spiritual maturity.
And we want that nourishment to reach more people.
More families.
More young believers.
More people struggling silently.
More Christians who cannot afford to purchase every resource they need.
More seekers who are beginning to ask serious questions about Jesus.
That work requires time, dedication, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe in its mission.
So I want to make a sincere invitation.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
The context emphasizes willing, purposeful generosity rather than giving under compulsion.
That matters deeply to us.
It does not replace faith, repentance, prayer, obedience, or service to your local church.
And it should never come at the expense of your family's essential needs.
But it can become one practical expression of your desire to help make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to others.
Think of the believer who finds a free devotional at exactly the moment they are ready to give up.
Think of the person who opens a Gospel-centered article after years of avoiding anything connected to Christianity.
Think of the family that discovers free books they can study together.
Think of the new Christian who needs help understanding Scripture but has no idea where to begin.
We cannot promise how God will use every resource.
But we can faithfully plant, teach, encourage, and point people to Jesus.
There is room in this mission for people who give financially and people who help in other ways.
We are grateful for both.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience that admires a page.
It is about pointing people to a Savior who deserves our worship, obedience, and love.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Has “love everyone” been twisted into “affirm everything”?
In many conversations, yes.
But we must not correct that distortion by creating another one.
The answer to counterfeit compassion is not cruelty.
The answer to moral compromise is not self-righteousness.
The answer to confusion is not contempt.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
The One who welcomed sinners without celebrating sin.
The One who confronted hypocrisy without abandoning mercy.
The One who spoke truth even when crowds walked away.
The One who gave His life for people who could never earn His love.
The One who rose again and still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer whether the world has misunderstood love.
Perhaps the question is whether we have allowed Jesus to teach us how to love.
Because somewhere tonight, a person is afraid to walk into church because they believe Christians will only see their past.
Somewhere, another person is sitting comfortably in a destructive pattern because nobody who loves them has been willing to speak honestly.
Somewhere, a believer is carrying shame that Christ is calling them to bring into the light.
Somewhere, a religious person is polishing the stones they intend to throw, forgetting how much mercy they themselves have received.
And somewhere, the Gospel is still announcing the same astonishing invitation.
Come to Christ.
Bring your sin into His light.
Receive His mercy through faith.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Follow the Savior who gave Himself for you.
You do not have to pretend your darkness is light.
And you do not have to believe your darkness is greater than His grace.
Jesus does not love you because your sin is harmless. He loves you so deeply that He gave Himself to save you from it.
That is the love worth proclaiming.
That is the truth worth standing for.
That is the grace worth sharing.
And that is why we will keep pointing people beyond the scandal of their past toward the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
The stones people remember throwing may tell the story of your shame, but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus proclaim that shame does not have to be the final chapter.
